sections.title: Name and cap
sections.text: Russula nitida (Pers.) Fr. is a small brittlegill, usually 2–8 cm across. The cap is convex at first, then expands and often becomes depressed in the centre. Its smooth cuticle is glossy and viscid in wet weather, more matte as it dries, and partly peelable. Colours range from vinaceous red, carmine-pink and violet to dark purple, sometimes with olive discoloration. The margin becomes distinctly striate with age.

sections.title: Gills, stem and spores
sections.text: The gills are rather widely spaced, pale cream at first and later ochre, sometimes with a pink edge near the cap margin. The fragile white stem may be flushed pink, especially towards the base; it can become spongy or hollow with age. The white flesh is brittle, with a faint fruity smell; its taste is described as mild. The spore deposit is ochre to yellow-ochre. Spores are subglobose to broadly ellipsoid and bear prominent warts, a character that requires microscopic examination.

sections.title: Habitat and taxonomy
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal brittlegill is associated mainly with birch (Betula). It fruits in summer and autumn in damp woods, often among Sphagnum, on poor sandy or peaty soils; it has also been recorded in mixed stands. Alder may occur at some collection sites, but the ecological references consulted do not identify it as the primary host. Taxonomic databases do not all delimit Russula nitida and R. sphagnophila in the same way; this entry follows the concept used by Species Fungorum and the European descriptions consulted.

sections.title: Identification and safety
sections.text: Cap colour alone cannot identify a brittlegill, and related species can look similar. A reliable identification may require examining the spores and other microscopic characters. Edibility has not been assessed here: do not eat a specimen based on this entry or its illustration.

traits: Smooth cap, glossy and viscid in wet weather, vinaceous-red to pink or violet, often depressed and striate at maturity
Rather widely spaced gills, pale cream then ochre; fragile white stem, sometimes flushed pink at the base
White brittle flesh; ochre to yellow-ochre spore deposit; strongly warted spores
Ectomycorrhizal brittlegill mainly associated with birch, often in damp woods and Sphagnum
Russula nitida is treated differently from R. sphagnophila by some taxonomic databases
safetyNote: Edibility has not been assessed in this entry. Brittlegills can be difficult to distinguish, and this description cannot confirm a collected specimen. Do not eat a mushroom identified from this entry or plate alone.
